questions.stem: Where does Sybylla spend her early childhood, before the family moves?
options: At Barney's Gap, the farm her father bought when she was a baby
At Bruggabrong, her father's prosperous station out by Timlinbilly
At Caddagat, her grandmother's homestead where she was born
At Five-Bob Downs, the station that belongs to the Beecham family
questions.explanation: Sybylla remembers Bruggabrong as a time of wealth and freedom, riding with the musterers. Losing it sets up the contrast with the poverty that follows.

questions.stem: Why does Sybylla hate life at Possum Gully?
options: It is Barney's Gap, where she must teach the M'Swat children
It is a rich estate where she is treated as a servant girl
It is a dull, poor dairy farm where life is hard and narrow
It is a busy town where she is kept indoors and cannot ride
questions.explanation: Her father sells his stations and buys Possum Gully, a small farm near Goulburn. Sybylla finds the flat landscape and endless milking a bitter come-down.

questions.stem: What happens to Dick Melvyn, Sybylla's father, at Possum Gully?
options: He leaves for the goldfields and the family hears nothing from him for years
His dealing fails and he takes to drink, sinking the family into debt
He is injured in a fall from his horse and can no longer work the farm
He sells the farm to Harold Beecham and goes to work for him as a drover
questions.explanation: Bad business and drought ruin him, and he begins to drink heavily. Sybylla has to fetch him home from the pubs, and the family's slide into poverty drives the plot.

questions.stem: Who invites Sybylla to live at Caddagat?
options: Her mother's friend, Mrs M'Swat
Her uncle, Julius Bossier
Her grandmother, Mrs Bossier
Her aunt, Miss Augusta Beecham
questions.explanation: Her mother's mother writes asking for Sybylla. Caddagat, with its comfort, music and books, is everything Possum Gully is not.

questions.stem: When Everard Grey hears Sybylla sing and act, what does he suggest?
options: That she should write for a Sydney paper
That she should be trained for the stage
That she should be sent to a ladies' college
That she should marry Frank Hawden soon
questions.explanation: Everard thinks she has real talent, but Grannie forbids any talk of the stage, which she sees as unrespectable. It is one of several doors closed to Sybylla.

questions.stem: What does Sybylla do when Harold Beecham first proposes to her?
options: Asks him to wait until she has asked her father
Strikes him across the face with a riding-whip
Accepts at once and tells her grandmother the news
Laughs at him and runs off to tell her aunt Helen
questions.explanation: Harold proposes at Five-Bob Downs on the night of the races and stoops to kiss her. Sybylla lashes out, then is ashamed of what she has done, while Harold says it does not matter.

questions.stem: What happens to Harold's fortune while Sybylla is at Caddagat?
options: He spends it on Caddagat, and Sybylla feels she has to accept him
He loses it, and Sybylla promises to marry him even if he is poor
He doubles it, and Sybylla refuses him because she fears his wealth
He loses it, and Sybylla breaks off their understanding at once
questions.explanation: When Harold loses his money, pity moves Sybylla to promise she will marry him at twenty-one, 'if you are as poor as a crow'. She later mocks her own conceit.

questions.stem: Why is Sybylla sent to work at Barney's Gap?
options: To earn money for her sister Gertie's schooling
To keep her away from Harold Beecham for a year
To learn farm work before she inherits Caddagat
To pay the interest on her father's loan from M'Swat
questions.explanation: Her mother's letter tells her she must be governess to the M'Swat children because her father owes M'Swat money. It is a sudden fall from Caddagat's comfort.

questions.stem: How does Sybylla's time at Barney's Gap end?
options: She falls ill with nervous exhaustion and is sent home to Possum Gully
She runs away at night and walks back to her grandmother at Caddagat
She marries young Peter M'Swat to settle her father's debt for good
She is rescued by Harold, who pays the debt and takes her to Five-Bob
questions.explanation: The dirt, ignorance and loneliness wear her down until she collapses. A doctor is called, and M'Swat writes to her parents to have her sent home.

questions.stem: Why is Sybylla's return to Possum Gully made harder by her sister Gertie?
options: Gertie marries Harold, the man Sybylla had promised to wed
Gertie takes Sybylla's job at Barney's Gap and is happy there
Gertie tells their mother that Sybylla had been idle at Caddagat
Gertie is sent to Caddagat in her place and soon forgets her
questions.explanation: Pretty, easy-going Gertie goes to Caddagat, and her letters show Sybylla is 'utterly forgotten'. Sybylla feels the unfairness of a world that rewards charm.

questions.stem: How does the novel end for Sybylla and Harold?
options: Harold marries Sybylla's sister, and Sybylla leaves to go on stage
Harold proposes again, and Sybylla accepts on condition she can write
Harold proposes again at Possum Gully, and Sybylla refuses him
Harold and Sybylla marry quietly and go to live at Five-Bob Downs
questions.explanation: Harold's fortune is restored and he comes to Possum Gully to ask again. Sybylla refuses, believing she would make him unhappy, and the novel ends with her still at home.

questions.stem: The novel opens with an introduction addressed to 'fellow Australians' and closes with a chapter dated 25 March 1899. What is the effect of this frame?
options: It reveals that an older Sybylla has become a famous Sydney writer
It frames the book as a romance that will end in Sybylla's marriage
It presents the book as Sybylla's own account, told to her country
It shows that Sybylla is writing chiefly for English readers abroad
questions.explanation: Sybylla speaks to her readers directly at both ends, as a young bush girl writing her life. The frame makes the book feel like a personal 'yarn' rather than a polished novel.

questions.stem: Sybylla Melvyn is best described as:
options: a wealthy, spoilt girl who scorns the people of the bush
a calm, practical girl who is content with farm life
a proud, restless, clever girl who believes she is plain
a quiet, gentle, obedient girl who longs to marry well
questions.explanation: Sybylla is talented, outspoken and moody, and convinced she is ugly. Her belief that no one could love a plain girl shapes how she treats Harold.

questions.stem: Harold Beecham is best described as:
options: a quiet, strong, wealthy squatter who is patient with Sybylla
a clever, witty Sydney barrister who encourages her to act
a lazy English jackeroo who makes a foolish proposal
a poor, bitter drover who resents the Bossier family
questions.explanation: Harold owns Five-Bob Downs. He is steady and good-natured, and stays loyal to Sybylla through her moods, his own ruin and her final refusal.

questions.stem: Who is Aunt Helen?
options: Harold's aunt at Five-Bob, who runs his household for him
Sybylla's strict aunt at Possum Gully, who hates the bush
The governess at Caddagat, who teaches Sybylla to sing
Sybylla's kind aunt at Caddagat, whose husband left her
questions.explanation: Aunt Helen is gentle and wise and helps Sybylla to think better of herself. Her husband deserted her, and her unhappy marriage is one of several in the novel that make Sybylla wary of marrying.

questions.stem: What is the role of Frank Hawden, the young jackeroo at Caddagat?
options: A wealthy squatter whose proposal Sybylla answers with a whip
A drover who brings news from Possum Gully to Caddagat
A comic suitor whose proposal Sybylla rejects with scorn
A wise friend who persuades Sybylla to marry Harold
questions.explanation: Frank meets Sybylla on her way to Caddagat and later proposes. His unwanted attention is played for comedy and shows how little Sybylla wants to be courted.

questions.stem: How does the novel present Sybylla's mother?
options: As gentle and loving, shielding Sybylla from her father's temper
As a wealthy woman who keeps her money from her husband and children
As proud of Sybylla's gifts, urging her toward an artistic career in the city
As worn down by poverty and a hard marriage, and often harsh with Sybylla
questions.explanation: Mrs Melvyn was raised in comfort and now struggles with debt and a drinking husband. She sends Sybylla to Barney's Gap and scolds her often, but the novel shows how hardship made her so.

questions.stem: When was My Brilliant Career first published?
options: In 1901, with a preface by Henry Lawson
In 1911, with a preface by Banjo Paterson
In 1891, with a preface by Henry Lawson
In 1921, with a preface by Banjo Paterson
questions.explanation: Lawson read the manuscript, wrote a preface and took it to his publishers in Edinburgh. It appeared in 1901, the year the Australian colonies federated.

questions.stem: Why is it significant that the book appeared in 1901?
options: It came out as Australia federated, when a national identity was being argued over
It came out just as women had won the vote in every Australian colony
It came out at the height of the gold rushes, when the bush was booming
It came out after the 1890s depression had ended, when bush farms were prospering again
questions.explanation: Sybylla's pride in being 'an Australian' and her sympathy for bush workers fit a time when writers were asking what Australia was. Federation was on 1 January 1901.

questions.stem: Franklin was distressed that readers took the novel as fact. What did she do?
options: She cut the passages about her family for a revised second edition
She moved to London and refused to discuss the book for the rest of her life
She would not let it be reprinted, and it returned only after her death
She had later editions printed with a note insisting it was fiction
questions.explanation: Many characters seemed close to her own family and neighbours. The novel was withdrawn until after she died in 1954 and was reissued in 1966.

questions.stem: What does the novel show about the 1890s in the bush?
options: The gold rushes had made small selectors in the bush wealthy and secure
Bush life was hard, but squatters and selectors shared the hardship equally
Drought mainly hurt the rich squatters, while small farmers coped well
Drought, debt and hard physical work could ruin small farming families
questions.explanation: The Melvyns lose stock in the drought of 1894-95 and live by dairying. Franklin shows the grind of farm life without romance.

questions.stem: How does My Brilliant Career connect to the idea of the 'New Woman' of the 1890s?
options: Sybylla finds fulfilment in managing a household and a busy station
Sybylla campaigns publicly for women's suffrage in New South Wales
Sybylla wants a life and career of her own, not a future defined by marriage
Sybylla marries for love rather than for money, just as the New Woman ideal demanded
questions.explanation: The New Woman sought independence and work beyond the home. Sybylla's refusal to marry and her longing for an artistic career reflect those debates.

questions.stem: Which idea is most central to My Brilliant Career?
options: The danger of education, which makes girls unhappy with country life
A young woman's struggle for independence in a world with few choices for her
The rewards of patient hard work for families who live on the land
The romance of a girl who slowly learns to love the man she had at first rejected
questions.explanation: Sybylla longs for art and freedom, but her sex, poverty and family hold her back. Her refusals of marriage are her way of keeping some independence.

questions.stem: Why does Sybylla refuse to marry Harold at the end?
options: She has discovered that Harold has lied to her about the loss of his money
She has promised her mother never to marry a man from the Beecham family
She has fallen in love with Everard Grey and plans to join him in Sydney
She believes she would make him unhappy and would lose herself in marriage
questions.explanation: She tells Harold, 'I am not good enough to be your wife, Hal, or that of any man.' Her refusal mixes low self-worth with a real fear of the life marriage offers women.

questions.stem: How does the novel present marriage?
options: As a romantic goal, shown by Sybylla's longing for the right man
As a risky trap for women, shown by the unhappy marriages around Sybylla
As the reward a good woman earns, shown by Aunt Helen's happy home
As a partnership of equals, shown by her parents' happiness in their early years
questions.explanation: Sybylla sees her mother worn down and Aunt Helen deserted. She fears marriage will mean drudgery and losing herself, which is why she keeps refusing.

questions.stem: How does the novel treat class?
options: It treats class lightly, as a source of comedy rather than conflict
It contrasts the culture of Caddagat with the squalor and ignorance of the M'Swats
It shows wealth bringing culture, since M'Swat is the poorest man in the whole district
It celebrates the squatters as the natural leaders of bush society
questions.explanation: Sybylla moves between a cultured squatter's home and the M'Swats' squalid farm, though M'Swat is not poor: he boasts of his bank account. She sympathises with bush workers, yet she is also snobbish, which a careful essay notes.

questions.stem: The title is My Brilliant Career, but Sybylla ends the novel at home with no career. What is the effect?
options: The title is literal, since Sybylla becomes a well-known actress by the end
The title is prophetic, since Sybylla is clearly destined for fame
The title is sincere, celebrating the brilliant freedom of bush life
The title is ironic, showing how little room there was for a girl's ambition
questions.explanation: Sybylla dreams of art but ends back at Possum Gully, in the narrow life she hates. The gap between the grand title and her real prospects is bitterly ironic.

questions.stem: Who narrates My Brilliant Career?
options: Harold, telling the story of the girl who refused him
An all-knowing narrator who moves between the characters
Sybylla's mother, explaining her daughter's choices
Sybylla, in the first person, looking back over recent years
questions.explanation: Sybylla tells her own story. Her voice is lively, opinionated and often contradictory, so readers must judge how far to trust her view of herself.

questions.stem: In the introduction Sybylla says the book is 'not a romance' but 'simply a yarn'. What does this suggest?
options: It will be a history of the district, told through official records
It will be an honest, plain-spoken story, not a dreamy love story
It will be a comic tall tale that no reader should take seriously
It will be a romance novel in which the heroine marries at the end
questions.explanation: A 'yarn' is an Australian bush tale. Sybylla rejects the conventions of romance, which prepares readers for a heroine who refuses to marry.

questions.stem: Sybylla often contradicts herself, mocks her own conceit and changes her mind. How should a reader respond?
options: Accept her judgements of herself, since she knows her own feelings best
Read her as an all-knowing narrator who sees the other characters clearly
Assume Franklin made errors, since she wrote the novel as a teenager
Treat her as a partly unreliable narrator whose self-judgements need testing
questions.explanation: Sybylla calls herself ugly and worthless, yet others admire her. Her contradictions are part of the characterisation, showing a young person unsure of who she is.

questions.stem: Many chapter titles, such as 'Possum Gully Left Behind. Hurrah! Hurrah!', are playful or ironic. What do they add?
options: They show Sybylla's lively, self-mocking voice shaping the story
They summarise the plot in neutral terms for the busy reader
They foreshadow a romantic ending in which Sybylla marries Harold
They create an impersonal tone that distances us from Sybylla
questions.explanation: Titles like this sound like Sybylla talking. They add humour and remind us that the story is filtered through her personality.

questions.stem: How does Franklin use contrasting settings?
options: Possum Gully and Caddagat show the difference between bush and city life
Bruggabrong and Possum Gully show the family's steady rise in wealth
The bush and Sydney show Sybylla's escape to a stage career in the city
Caddagat's comfort and Barney's Gap's squalor show Sybylla's rise and fall
questions.explanation: Possum Gully, Caddagat, Five-Bob Downs and Barney's Gap are moral and social worlds. Moving between them shows how much Sybylla's fate depends on money and family.

questions.stem: Who says 'I make no apologies for being egotistical'?
options: Sybylla, in the introduction to her story
Harold, after Sybylla calls him conceited
Everard, defending his advice about the stage
Grannie, scolding Sybylla for her vanity
questions.explanation: Sybylla announces at the start that the book is 'all about myself'. It sets up her frank, self-centred, self-mocking voice.

questions.stem: In Chapter Seven Sybylla says that being a girl was pleasant 'until a hideous truth dawned upon me', that she was ugly. What does this belief lead to?
options: It makes her stay away from Caddagat so that no one will look at her
It makes her train as an actress so that she can learn to look pretty
It makes her doubt that anyone could truly love her, including Harold
It makes her give up her ambitions and agree to marry the first suitor
questions.explanation: Her conviction that she is plain runs through the novel. She cannot believe Harold loves her, which feeds her harshness and her refusals.

questions.stem: When Sybylla says 'I will marry you when I am twenty-one if you are as poor as a crow', what is happening?
options: Harold has asked her to the races, and she is only teasing him
Harold has just lost his fortune, and pity moves her to promise
Harold has just regained his fortune, and she is finally won over
Harold has asked her father's consent, and she defies her family
questions.explanation: The promise comes when Harold is ruined. She later mocks herself for it, and when he is rich again she refuses him.

questions.stem: 'I am proud that I am an Australian, a daughter of the Southern Cross, a child of the mighty bush.' What does this line from the last chapter show?
options: Her deep pride in Australia, despite all the hardship of bush life
Her wish to leave Australia and seek her fortune in London instead
Her anger at the bush, which she blames for her family's ruin
Her pride in her family's wealth and their position in society
questions.explanation: The closing chapter praises Australian workers and the bush. Sybylla can hate the drudgery of farm life and still love her country.

questions.stem: Sybylla tells Harold, 'I am not good enough to be your wife, Hal, or that of any man.' What tension does this line reveal?
options: Her refusal is a joke, which Harold fails to understand and resents
Her refusal is both low self-worth and a wish to stay free of marriage
Her refusal is a test, since she expects him to ask again the next day
Her refusal is a lie, since she has secretly agreed to marry Everard
questions.explanation: She puts herself down, yet the words 'or that of any man' show she rejects marriage itself. A good essay discusses both readings.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the prompt 'Sybylla's greatest enemy is herself.' Discuss.
options: My Brilliant Career is a novel by Miles Franklin that was first published in 1901
This essay will discuss whether Sybylla is her own enemy in My Brilliant Career
Sybylla Melvyn lives at Possum Gully and is sent to her grandmother at Caddagat
Franklin suggests that Sybylla's belief in her own ugliness does as much damage as poverty
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence names the author, takes a position on the prompt and says what the paragraph will prove. The others give facts, announce or retell.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'At Barney's Gap the house is dirty and the children are rude.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: Quote Sybylla's whole description of the dirty house and the rude M'Swat children
Describe Sybylla's journey to Barney's Gap, stop by stop, in more detail
Explain how the squalor shows Sybylla's fall and the narrow life she is trapped in
State that Barney's Gap is an important setting in the novel
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what the evidence suggests. Linking the setting to class and to Sybylla's limited choices connects it to the novel's ideas.
